sentences.summary: det_07: The 'new-manager bounce' folk theory. Source: Why sacking the manager rarely works — The Guardian (https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2014/jan/30/sacking-managers-research-) Facts: Statistical analyses repeatedly find no 'bounce' beyond what regression to the mean predicts

raw_evidence.label: The 'new-manager bounce' folk theory
raw_evidence.content: Fans and pundits frequently invoke a 'new-manager bounce' — the idea that a fresh face injects energy and lifts results in the short term. Empirical work has repeatedly shown the bounce is almost entirely a statistical artifact: a team that has just sacked its coach was, by definition, underperforming, and underperforming teams tend to drift back toward their long-run mean regardless of whether the coach changes. The Economist's analysis goes further by quantifying how much regression to the mean a manager's record exhibits — it found that an extraordinary 461 games of league-average performance must be 'added' to any manager's actual record to produce the best forecast of his next job, meaning a single-season tenure of 38 games carries only about 8% predictive weight.

raw_evidence.label: Most over-performing team-seasons (Leicester 2016 leads)
raw_evidence.content: Leicester City's 2015-16 Premier League title-winning season is the most extreme team-season in the entire dataset, beating its FIFA-rating-based forecast by +1.07 points per game — across 38 games, that is roughly 41 extra league points. RB Leipzig's 2017 Bundesliga campaign is second (+0.92), Liverpool 2019 third (+0.87 ppg). On the underperforming side, Monaco 2019 was the biggest collapse (-0.91 ppg), followed by Chelsea's post-title 2016 season (-0.83). The presence of Dortmund 2015 in the bottom five is sobering: that was Klopp's farewell campaign, and even his Dortmund missed expectations badly that one season.

sources.title: Why sacking the manager rarely works — The Guardian
facts: Statistical analyses repeatedly find no 'bounce' beyond what regression to the mean predicts

raw_evidence.label: The headline distribution: most managers cluster around zero
raw_evidence.content: Across 502 manager-tenures of at least one full season, the average manager added 0.04 points per game above what FIFA-based player ratings predicted — a margin so close to zero it is statistically indistinguishable from luck for any single tenure. The standard deviation is 0.18 points-per-game; the 5th-95th percentile range runs only from -0.24 to +0.34. About 45% of all tenures fall within ±0.10 ppg of expectation. Just 16% of managers cleared +0.20 ppg over a full-season-or-more sample, and only a handful exceeded +0.40. This is the spine of the story: the typical manager is a rounding error.
raw_evidence.code:
# use current_tenure stats
big = tenures.dropna(subset=['current_tenure_total_games', 'current_tenure_points_per_game_above_expectation'])
big = big[big['current_tenure_total_games'] >= 38]
ppg_above = big['current_tenure_points_per_game_above_expectation']
print(f"Tenures with >=38 games: {len(big)}")
print(f"Mean ppg-above-expectation: {ppg_above.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Median ppg-above-expectation: {ppg_above.median():.4f}")
print(f"Std: {ppg_above.std():.4f}")
print(f"5th pct: {ppg_above.quantile(0.05):.4f}")
print(f"95th pct: {ppg_above.quantile(0.95):.4f}")
print(f"Min/Max: {ppg_above.min():.4f} / {ppg_above.max():.4f}")

# Histogram bins for distribution chart
bins = np.arange(-1.0, 1.05, 0.10)
counts, edges = np.histogram(ppg_above, bins=bins)
print("\nHistogram (bin_left, count):")
for c, e in zip(counts, edges[:-1]):
    print(f"  [{e:+.2f}, {e+0.10:+.2f}): {c}")

# How many managers actually clear a meaningful threshold?
print(f"\nTenures with > +0.20 ppg-above-expectation: {(ppg_above > 0.20).sum()} ({100*(ppg_above > 0.20).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"Tenures with > +0.10 ppg-above-expectation: {(ppg_above > 0.10).sum()} ({100*(ppg_above > 0.10).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"Tenures within +/-0.10 ppg of expectation: {((ppg_above.abs() <= 0.10)).sum()} ({100*((ppg_above.abs() <= 0.10)).mean():.1f}%)")

# --- ana_04: top 12 and bottom 6 manager-tenures by ppg above expectation ---
print("\n=== ana_04 ===")
raw_evidence.output:
Tenures with >=38 games: 502
Mean ppg-above-expectation: 0.0430
Median ppg-above-expectation: 0.0373
Std: 0.1756
5th pct: -0.2381
95th pct: 0.3384
Min/Max: -0.6593 / 0.5740
Tenures with > +0.20 ppg-above-expectation: 80 (15.9%)
Tenures with > +0.10 ppg-above-expectation: 183 (36.5%)
Tenures within +/-0.10 ppg of expectation: 224 (44.6%)

raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Economist's 2019 manager analysis
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Economist's January 2019 Graphic Detail article 'Managers in football matter much less than most fans think.' The Economist's data team built a forecasting model using FIFA video-game player ratings to estimate how many points each squad in Europe's 'big five' leagues — England, Spain, Germany, Italy and France — should win in a season based purely on player skill. They then compared each team's actual results to these expectations to isolate the manager's contribution. The analysis covered 15 seasons of league fixtures from August 2004 through December 2018, and was deliberately framed against an industry that fires roughly 50 head coaches per top-flight season across these leagues.

raw_evidence.label: FIFA video-game ratings as a player-skill proxy
raw_evidence.content: The Economist used player ratings from EA Sports' FIFA video-game series, scraped from FIFAindex.com, as their measure of player ability. FIFA ratings combine objective performance data — shots, passes, tackles — with subjective evaluations from a panel of about 9,000 dedicated scouts. Worst regular top-flight starters score around 65; Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo can reach 95. The analysts chose FIFA ratings because they were the only publicly available skill estimate that did not depend on team results (unlike league standings or pundit ratings) and that covered at least ten years. To use these ratings as forecasts, they z-scored each player by season and position group (goalkeeper, defender, attacker), then exponentiated the z-scores so the gap between elite and merely good players grew non-linearly.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: how good is FIFA-rating-based forecasting?
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's forecast model, built only from preseason FIFA player ratings, achieved an average error of 7.7 points per team per season across 15 seasons in five leagues. For the most recent three English Premier League campaigns at the time, their model scored an average error of 8.5 points — only marginally worse than the 8.1-point average error of preseason betting markets, which incorporate professional gamblers' aggregate wisdom. This benchmark matters because it justifies treating the FIFA-derived expected points as a credible counterfactual against which manager overperformance can be measured.

raw_evidence.label: FIFA video-game ratings as a player-skill proxy
raw_evidence.content: The Economist used player ratings from EA Sports' FIFA video-game series, scraped from FIFAindex.com, as their measure of player ability. FIFA ratings combine objective performance data — shots, passes, tackles — with subjective evaluations from a panel of about 9,000 dedicated scouts. Worst regular top-flight starters score around 65; Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo can reach 95. The analysts chose FIFA ratings because they were the only publicly available skill estimate that did not depend on team results (unlike league standings or pundit ratings) and that covered at least ten years. To use these ratings as forecasts, they z-scored each player by season and position group (goalkeeper, defender, attacker), then exponentiated the z-scores so the gap between elite and merely good players grew non-linearly.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: how good is FIFA-rating-based forecasting?
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's forecast model, built only from preseason FIFA player ratings, achieved an average error of 7.7 points per team per season across 15 seasons in five leagues. raw_evidence.label: FIFA video-game ratings as a player-skill proxy
raw_evidence.content: The Economist used player ratings from EA Sports' FIFA video-game series, scraped from FIFAindex.com, as their measure of player ability. FIFA ratings combine objective performance data — shots, passes, tackles — with subjective evaluations from a panel of about 9,000 dedicated scouts. raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Economist's 2019 manager analysis
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Economist's January 2019 Graphic Detail article 'Managers in football matter much less than most fans think.' The Economist's data team built a forecasting model using FIFA video-game player ratings to estimate how many points each squad in Europe's 'big five' leagues — England, Spain, Germany, Italy and France — should win in a season based purely on player skill. They then compared each team's actual results to these expectations to isolate the manager's contribution. The analysis covered 15 seasons of league fixtures from August 2004 through December 2018, and was deliberately framed against an industry that fires roughly 50 head coaches per top-flight season across these leagues.

facts: Article published 2019-01-19 in The Economist's Graphic Detail column
Analysis covers Europe's big-five leagues: England, Spain, Germany, Italy, France
Time range: August 2004 to December 2018

raw_evidence.label: FIFA video-game ratings as a player-skill proxy
raw_evidence.content: The Economist used player ratings from EA Sports' FIFA video-game series, scraped from FIFAindex.com, as their measure of player ability. FIFA ratings combine objective performance data — shots, passes, tackles — with subjective evaluations from a panel of about 9,000 dedicated scouts. Worst regular top-flight starters score around 65; Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo can reach 95. The analysts chose FIFA ratings because they were the only publicly available skill estimate that did not depend on team results (unlike league standings or pundit ratings) and that covered at least ten years. To use these ratings as forecasts, they z-scored each player by season and position group (goalkeeper, defender, attacker), then exponentiated the z-scores so the gap between elite and merely good players grew non-linearly.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: how good is FIFA-rating-based forecasting?
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's forecast model, built only from preseason FIFA player ratings, achieved an average error of 7.7 points per team per season across 15 seasons in five leagues. For the most recent three English Premier League campaigns at the time, their model scored an average error of 8.5 points — only marginally worse than the 8.1-point average error of preseason betting markets, which incorporate professional gamblers' aggregate wisdom. This benchmark matters because it justifies treating the FIFA-derived expected points as a credible counterfactual against which manager overperformance can be measured.

raw_evidence.label: Coverage: 5 leagues, 15 seasons, 27,390 fixtures
raw_evidence.content: The dataset covers 27,390 individual league fixtures from Europe's big-five leagues — England, Spain, Italy, France, and Germany — across 15 seasons from August 2004 through May 2019. Forecast model errors averaged 7.27 points per team-season (median 5.99); the league-by-league mean absolute error ranges from a tight 7.01 in France to 7.50 in England. The Pearson correlation between expected and actual points-per-game across all 1,470 team-seasons is 0.796, confirming the FIFA-rating-based forecast tracks reality closely.

raw_evidence.label: Sir Alex Ferguson — the canonical outlier
raw_evidence.content: Sir Alex Ferguson managed Manchester United from November 1986 to June 2013, an extraordinary 27 years that included 13 Premier League titles, 2 UEFA Champions Leagues, and 5 FA Cups. He is the most-cited counter-example whenever someone argues that managers do not matter — and he is, indeed, an outlier in The Economist's data. But the data also makes clear that Ferguson is the *exception* that proves the rule: most of his peers, even celebrated ones, are statistically indistinguishable from a league-average coach once you account for squad quality.

raw_evidence.label: Academic evidence: mid-season sackings rarely help
raw_evidence.content: Multiple peer-reviewed studies in sports economics and management have found that mid-season manager dismissals do not, on average, improve team results once you control for the regression to the mean that would have happened anyway. A team that fires its coach is by definition underperforming; a team that underperforms tends to revert toward its expected level whether the coach is sacked or not. sources.title: Does Manager Turnover Improve Firm Performance? Evidence from Dutch Soccer (Ter Weel, 2011)
facts: Mid-season manager dismissals show no statistically significant performance gain over a matched control group
The apparent post-sacking 'bounce' is largely explained by regression to the mean

raw_evidence.label: The 'new-manager bounce' folk theory
raw_evidence.content: Fans and pundits frequently invoke a 'new-manager bounce' — the idea that a fresh face injects energy and lifts results in the short term. Empirical work has repeatedly shown the bounce is almost entirely a statistical artifact: a team that has just sacked its coach was, by definition, underperforming, and underperforming teams tend to drift back toward their long-run mean regardless of whether the coach changes. The Economist's analysis goes further by quantifying how much regression to the mean a manager's record exhibits — it found that an extraordinary 461 games of league-average performance must be 'added' to any manager's actual record to produce the best forecast of his next job, meaning a single-season tenure of 38 games carries only about 8% predictive weight.

sources.title: Why sacking the manager rarely works — The Guardian
facts: Statistical analyses repeatedly find no 'bounce' beyond what regression to the mean predicts

raw_evidence.label: The killer test: past overperformance barely predicts future
raw_evidence.content: Among 222 managers with at least two distinct tenures, the correlation between first-tenure and second-tenure points-per-game above expectation is just r = 0.04 (p = 0.54) — statistically indistinguishable from no relationship at all. The conditional probability that a manager who overperformed in tenure one will overperform again in tenure two is only 45%, barely better than the 36.6% rate observed for managers who underperformed in tenure one. The data refuses to grant managers a stable 'level of skill' that travels with them.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: tenure1 vs tenure2 — among managers with >=2 tenures, does overperformance carry? ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
two = seq.dropna(subset=['tenure1_above_expectation', 'tenure2_above_expectation'])
print(f"Managers with at least 2 tenures: {len(two)}")
print(f"  tenure1 > 0 (overperformed): {(two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0).sum()} ({100*(two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"  tenure2 > 0 (overperformed): {(two['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).sum()} ({100*(two['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.1f}%)")

# Conditional: of those who overperformed in tenure1, what fraction overperformed in tenure2?
over1 = two[two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0]
under1 = two[two['tenure1_above_expectation'] <= 0]
print(f"\nP(over in t2 | over in t1): {(over1['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.3f}  (n={len(over1)})")
print(f"P(over in t2 | under in t1): {(under1['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.3f}  (n={len(under1)})")

# Pearson correlation between tenure1 and tenure2 ppg-above-expectation
raw_evidence.output:
Managers with at least 2 tenures: 222
  tenure1 > 0 (overperformed): 129 (58.1%)
  tenure2 > 0 (overperformed): 92 (41.4%)
P(over in t2 | over in t1): 0.450  (n=129)
P(over in t2 | under in t1): 0.366  (n=93)
Pearson r (tenure1 vs tenure2 ppg-above): 0.041 (p=0.544)

raw_evidence.editorial_notes: r = 0.04 is the killer number; 45% vs 37% conditional probabilities back it up. The interactive should let readers select a manager and see their two tenures.

raw_evidence.label: The killer test: past overperformance barely predicts future
raw_evidence.content: Among 222 managers with at least two distinct tenures, the correlation between first-tenure and second-tenure points-per-game above expectation is just r = 0.04 (p = 0.54) — statistically indistinguishable from no relationship at all. The data refuses to grant managers a stable 'level of skill' that travels with them.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: tenure1 vs tenure2 — among managers with >=2 tenures, does overperformance carry? ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
two = seq.dropna(subset=['tenure1_above_expectation', 'tenure2_above_expectation'])
print(f"Managers with at least 2 tenures: {len(two)}")
print(f"  tenure1 > 0 (overperformed): {(two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0).sum()} ({100*(two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"  tenure2 > 0 (overperformed): {(two['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).sum()} ({100*(two['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.1f}%)")

# Conditional: of those who overperformed in tenure1, what fraction overperformed in tenure2?
over1 = two[two['tenure1_above_expectation'] > 0]
under1 = two[two['tenure1_above_expectation'] <= 0]
print(f"\nP(over in t2 | over in t1): {(over1['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.3f}  (n={len(over1)})")
print(f"P(over in t2 | under in t1): {(under1['tenure2_above_expectation'] > 0).mean():.3f}  (n={len(under1)})")

# Pearson correlation between tenure1 and tenure2 ppg-above-expectation

A three-season tenure (114 games) retains 19.8%. Ten seasons (380 games) retains 45.2%. Sir Alex Ferguson's data-covered tenure of 342 games retains 42.6%. Effectively, managers must work two decades before the model lets them speak for themselves.

raw_evidence.label: Sir Alex Ferguson — the canonical outlier
raw_evidence.content: Sir Alex Ferguson managed Manchester United from November 1986 to June 2013, an extraordinary 27 years that included 13 Premier League titles, 2 UEFA Champions Leagues, and 5 FA Cups. He is the most-cited counter-example whenever someone argues that managers do not matter — and he is, indeed, an outlier in The Economist's data. But the data also makes clear that Ferguson is the *exception* that proves the rule: most of his peers, even celebrated ones, are statistically indistinguishable from a league-average coach once you account for squad quality.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: clubs spend hundreds of millions on the wrong lever
raw_evidence.content: Top-flight clubs spend enormous sums hiring and firing managers — payoff settlements at top clubs routinely exceed £10 million, before counting the cost of the new hire's contract or any squad turnover the new boss demands. If managers add only a small amount of variance over and above what the squad's player-skill predicts, those firing decisions look closer to scapegoating than competitive strategy. The Economist's data offered the strongest publicly available evidence that fans and owners alike systematically overestimate manager impact, with implications for how clubs allocate resources.

raw_evidence.label: Most active managers project as below-average
raw_evidence.content: Of the 596 currently-employed-or-recently-employed managers in the database, 432 (72.5%) have a negative projection — meaning the model expects them to win fewer points per season than a hypothetical league-average coach with the same squad. Just 44 managers (7.4%) project as adding more than one point per season; 74 (12.4%) clear half a point. Half the population sits within ±0.5 points-per-season of league-average, which over a 38-game campaign is one decisive corner kick away from indistinguishable. The mean projection is -0.25, the median -0.36 — a heavily left-skewed distribution where most coaches do not earn their wage.

print(f"Std: {proj.std():.3f}")
print(f"Range: [{proj.min():.3f}, {proj.max():.3f}]")
print(f"Top 10% projection threshold: {proj.quantile(0.90):.3f}")
print(f"# with > 1.0 ppg added: {(proj > 1.0).sum()} ({100*(proj > 1.0).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"# with > 0.5 ppg added: {(proj > 0.5).sum()} ({100*(proj > 0.5).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"# negative (sub-average): {(proj < 0).sum()} ({100*(proj < 0).mean():.1f}%)")
print(f"# within +/-0.5 ppg added: {((proj.abs() <= 0.5)).sum()} ({100*((proj.abs() <= 0.5)).mean():.1f}%)")

sources.title: The Economist on manager impact (re-reported in The Guardian)
facts: Premier League clubs paid more than £90 million in manager severance during the 2018-19 season

raw_evidence.label: The 'new-manager bounce' folk theory
raw_evidence.content: Fans and pundits frequently invoke a 'new-manager bounce' — the idea that a fresh face injects energy and lifts results in the short term. Empirical work has repeatedly shown the bounce is almost entirely a statistical artifact: a team that has just sacked its coach was, by definition, underperforming, and underperforming teams tend to drift back toward their long-run mean regardless of whether the coach changes. The Economist's analysis goes further by quantifying how much regression to the mean a manager's record exhibits — it found that an extraordinary 461 games of league-average performance must be 'added' to any manager's actual record to produce the best forecast of his next job, meaning a single-season tenure of 38 games carries only about 8% predictive weight.

facts: Statistical analyses repeatedly find no 'bounce' beyond what regression to the mean predicts

raw_evidence.label: Close — what this does and does not say
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: Pure editorial close. Manager-severance figure (£90m, 2018-19) and 'post-sacking bounce as regression to the mean' are the two anchors. Do not introduce new statistics.
